key_terms.meaning: A lowpass signal bandlimited to fm can be rebuilt exactly from samples taken at fs ≥ 2fm.
The minimum sampling rate 2fm for a signal whose highest frequency is fm, in samples per second.
Folding of frequencies above fs/2 onto low frequencies when fs < 2fm, producing false in-band tones.
A lowpass filter before the sampler that removes all content above fs/2 so nothing can fold back.
Pulse amplitude modulation: the message sample sets the height of each periodic pulse.
Pulse width modulation: the message sample sets how long each pulse stays on; amplitude stays fixed.
Pulse position modulation: the message sample shifts the pulse away from its nominal slot position.
Replacing each sample value by the nearest of L fixed levels, so the value becomes one of a finite set.
For uniform steps of size Δ, error power is Δ²/12 when the error is equally likely anywhere in the step.
Compressing large amplitudes and expanding small ones before coding, so weak signals get finer steps and better SNR.
Pulse code modulation: each quantized sample is sent as an n-bit code word, so bit rate Rb = fs·n.
Differential PCM sends the quantized difference between the sample and a prediction from past samples.
Adaptive DPCM changes the quantizer step size or the predictor while running, to track a changing signal.
One bit per sample: the receiver staircase moves up by a step for bit 1 and down by a step for bit 0.
Distortion when the signal rises faster than the staircase can follow; fixed by a larger step or a faster clock.
Idle up-down toggling of the staircase around a flat signal, giving a small hiss in quiet passages.
One complete round of time slots in TDM, repeated at the sampling rate fs.
A short empty gap between TDM slots that absorbs timing jitter and keeps neighbouring channels from overlapping.
Line code that sends a transition in the middle of every bit; 1 and 0 use opposite directions, so there is no DC.
The distribution of a waveform's power over frequency, used to compare the bandwidth of line codes.

takeaways: Sampling at fs ≥ 2fm keeps all information; sampling slower folds high frequencies down as aliasing and the loss cannot be undone.
PAM, PWM and PPM all carry the message on a pulse train; PAM is easiest to build, PWM and PPM trade bandwidth for noise immunity.
Uniform quantization gives equal steps and error power Δ²/12; the SNR falls by 6 dB for every halving of signal amplitude.
Companding bends the step sizes so quiet talkers get as good an SNR as loud ones, which is why telephony uses μ-law or A-law.
PCM bit rate is fs·n, so 8 kHz sampling with 8 bits gives 64 kbit/s, the standard telephone channel.
DPCM and ADPCM send prediction error instead of the sample, and correlated speech makes that error much smaller than the sample.
Delta modulation is a 1-bit DPCM with a two-level quantizer; adaptive step size is what makes it usable on real speech.
TDM shares one link by giving every channel a fixed repeating slot, and the frame rate must equal the sampling rate.
Line codes trade DC content, clock recovery and bandwidth: Manchester is DC-free and self-clocking but needs twice the bandwidth of NRZ.
bank_note: Long answers are usually built around one full chain — anti-alias filter, sample, quantize, encode, multiplex, line code — so keep the numbers (fs, n, Rb, SNR, Δ²/12) attached to each block and sketch the waveforms.

bank.q: State the sampling theorem for a lowpass signal and explain with a spectrum sketch why sampling below 2fm produces aliasing that cannot be removed later.
outline: Define fm and fs; state fs ≥ 2fm and the Nyquist rate.
Spectrum of a sampled signal = copies of the baseband spectrum spaced by fs.
If fs < 2fm the copies overlap; the overlap is the alias.
Show a tone above fs/2 appearing at fs − f as a false low tone.
Note that once folded, no filter can separate the alias.

bank.q: Compare PAM, PWM and PPM on the message-carrying parameter, pulse amplitude, pulse width, bandwidth needed and noise immunity.
outline: PAM: amplitude varies, width and position fixed.
PWM: width varies, amplitude fixed.
PPM: position varies; obtained by differentiating PWM.
Bandwidth order: PAM < PWM < PPM.
Noise immunity order: PPM best, PAM worst.
Simple block diagrams of each modulator.

bank.q: Derive the quantization noise power Δ²/12 for a uniform quantizer and hence write the output SNR for a full-scale sinusoid.
outline: Error e lies in −Δ/2 to +Δ/2 with uniform density 1/Δ.
Mean square error = ∫e²(1/Δ)de over that range = Δ²/12.
Signal power for a sinusoid of amplitude A is A²/2.
SNR = (A²/2)/(Δ²/12) = 6A²/Δ².
With L levels and step Δ = 2A/L this gives SNR = 1.5L², about 6n dB for L = 2ⁿ.

bank.q: Explain PCM with a block diagram and define bit rate, bit duration and quantization error.
outline: Blocks: anti-alias filter, sampler, quantizer, encoder, channel, regenerator, decoder, reconstruction filter.
Sample rate fs ≥ 2fm; L = 2ⁿ levels; Rb = fs·n.
Bit duration Tb = 1/Rb; channel bandwidth roughly Rb/2.
Quantization noise Δ²/12 and its SNR.
Why regeneration in repeatered PCM gives near error-free transmission.

bank.q: Explain DPCM and ADPCM, and show how a predictor reduces the bits needed for speech.
outline: Predicted value from past reconstructed samples, error = sample − prediction.
Quantize and transmit the error; receiver rebuilds the sample.
Correlated signal makes error variance much smaller, so fewer levels give the same SNR.
ADPCM adapts step size or predictor gain to the short-term signal power.
Typical saving: 2 to 4 bits per sample over PCM.

bank.q: Describe delta modulation, and define slope overload and granular noise.
outline: 1-bit encoder; staircase moves ±Δ once per sample.
Conditions: step Δ and sampling fs must satisfy Δ·fs ≥ 2π·fm·A for no overload.
Slope overload: signal slope exceeds Δ·fs.
Granular noise: flat signal causes up-down toggling.
Adaptive DM varies Δ to reduce both.

bank.q: A speech signal is bandlimited to 3.4 kHz and sampled at 8 kHz with 8-bit uniform PCM. Find the bit rate, the first-null bandwidth and the SNR in dB for a full-scale sinusoid.
outline: Rb = fs·n = 8000 × 8 = 64 kbit/s.
Nyquist rate 6.8 kHz < 8 kHz so no aliasing.
Bandwidth ≈ Rb/2 = 32 kHz for a polar NRZ null-to-null.
Quick rule: SNR ≈ 6n + 1.8 dB.

bank.q: Sixteen PCM channels, each sampled at 8 kHz with 8 bits per sample, are time division multiplexed. Find the frame duration, the slot width and the line bit rate, and say how much guard time you would keep.
outline: Frame duration = 1/fs = 125 µs.
Bits per frame = 16 × 8 = 128 bits.
Slot width = 125 µs/16 = 7.8125 µs.
Slot holds 8 bits; a small guard time or one sync bit per frame absorbs jitter.
Add synchronisation bits and recompute if asked.

bank.q: A 4 kHz lowpass signal is sampled at 6 kHz. A 3 kHz interferer is present at the input. Find the alias frequency and state the design change that removes it.
outline: fs = 6 kHz, so fs/2 = 3 kHz; the interferer sits exactly at the fold point.
Any tone at f > fs/2 folds to fs − f; a tone at 3 kHz maps to 3 kHz (fold point).
Use a second example, e.g. a 5 kHz tone folding to 6 − 5 = 1 kHz.
Place an anti-alias lowpass at about 3 kHz before the sampler.
Raising fs also helps but costs bit rate.

bank.q: For an 8-bit PCM system with a full-scale range of ±2 V, find the step size, the maximum quantization error and the noise power, and compare with a 12-bit system.
outline: L = 256, total range 4 V, Δ = 4/256 = 15.6 mV.
Maximum error = Δ/2 = 7.8 mV.
Noise power = Δ²/12 ≈ 2.03 × 10⁻⁵ W, i.e. 20.3 µW.
12 bits: Δ = 4/4096 ≈ 0.98 mV, noise power ≈ 7.9 × 10⁻⁸ W.
Every extra bit is 6 dB better SNR.

bank.q: Sketch the waveforms of NRZ-L, RZ, Manchester and differential Manchester for the bit stream 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 and comment on clock recovery and DC content.
outline: NRZ-L: level held for the full bit, level change only on data change.
RZ: pulse in the first half of the bit, zero for the second half.
Manchester: mid-bit transition, low-to-high for 1, high-to-low for 0 (state convention).
Differential Manchester: data in the presence or absence of a start-of-bit transition, always a mid-bit transition.
Manchester and RZ have a spectral line at the bit rate, so clock recovery is easy.
Manchester and RZ have little DC; NRZ can drift.

bank.q: Compare PCM, DPCM and delta modulation for speech on the basis of bit rate, complexity, SNR and behaviour on quiet passages.
outline: PCM at 64 kbit/s gives about 6n dB SNR and is simple but wasteful on redundancy.
DPCM saves 2 to 4 bits per sample at equal quality.
DM at 1 bit per sample needs a high clock (tens of kHz) and shows slope overload and granular noise.
ADPCM and ADM solve the quiet-signal problem by adapting the step.
Complexity order: DM < DPCM < ADPCM < PCM with companding.
Recommend by application: telephony uses companded PCM or ADPCM, local links use DM.

bank.q: Explain why companding is used in speech PCM. Draw the μ-law and A-law compression curves and compare the SNR for weak and strong talkers.
outline: Uniform PCM SNR falls by 6 dB each time signal amplitude halves, so quiet talkers get poor quality.
Companding gives small amplitudes fine steps and large amplitudes coarse steps.
μ-law: y = sgn(x)·ln(1 + μ|x|)/ln(1 + μ), μ = 255 in North America and Japan.
A-law: piecewise linear, A = 87.6, used in Europe and much of the world.
Quantization noise becomes roughly proportional to signal power, so SNR stays near-constant over a wide range.
Cost: extra hardware or software, and a slight idle-channel noise floor.

bank.q: Design a TDM-PCM system for 30 telephone channels. Choose sampling rate, bits per sample, frame structure with synchronisation, and line bit rate; discuss guard time and timing jitter.
outline: fs = 8 kHz, frame = 125 µs, 8 bits per channel.
30 voice channels plus one sync channel gives 31 slots, 8 bits each = 248 bits per frame.
Rb = 248/125 µs ≈ 1.984 Mbit/s; rounding to 2.048 Mbit/s is the standard E1 figure.
Slot width = 125/32 = 3.9 µs when a 32-slot frame is used.
Guard time absorbs jitter between multiplexer and demultiplexer clocks.
Sync word must be chosen to avoid false locking; discuss jitter accumulation with many repeaters.

glossary.def: Converting a continuous-time signal into a sequence of values taken at instants spaced Ts = 1/fs apart.
fs/2, the highest frequency a sampler can represent without aliasing.
PAM in which the pulse keeps the shape of the original waveform during the on time.
PAM in which each pulse is a rectangle whose height equals the sample; needs an equaliser for the aperture effect.
Slight amplitude droop caused by holding the sample over the pulse width, corrected by a sinc equaliser.
A device that maps a continuous range of sample values onto L discrete output levels.
The gap Δ between two neighbouring quantization levels.
Quantization whose steps are small near zero and large at high amplitude.
Logarithmic companding law with μ = 255 used for speech PCM in North America and Japan.
Piecewise-logarithmic companding law with A = 87.6 used in European and many other telephone networks.
The n-bit binary number that represents one quantized sample in PCM.
A PCM receiver-transmitter pair that decides each bit and retransmits a clean pulse, so noise does not accumulate.
The difference between the actual sample and the value predicted from earlier samples; this is what DPCM sends.
A filter that forms the estimate of the current sample from a weighted sum of past reconstructed samples.
The granular noise heard when the input is silent in delta modulation or DPCM.
A step size that grows when the encoder makes repeated same-direction decisions and shrinks when it alternates.
One complete set of time slots, one per channel, repeated every 1/fs seconds.
A fixed bit pattern in each TDM frame that lets the receiver find the slot boundaries.
Line code that uses one polarity and zero, so it has a non-zero average and a DC component.
Line code that uses both positive and negative levels, so the average is zero for balanced data.
Three-level code in which successive marks alternate in polarity (also called AMI).
A line code whose waveform always contains transitions from which the receiver can recover the bit clock.
The minimum baseband bandwidth Rb/2 needed to send Rb bits per second without intersymbol interference.
The number of bits sent per second, in bits per second (bit/s).
